question: What is the nominal voltage of the DA40 electrical system?

options.text: 12 volt DC
28 volt DC
115 volt AC
270 volt DC

explanation: The DA40 uses a 28 volt DC system fed by an engine-driven alternator, with a 24 volt battery as the standby source. Any replacement battery, ground power unit or portable equipment must match this 28 volt architecture - connecting a 12 volt ground power unit is not acceptable.
reference: Airplane Flight Manual, Section 7 - Electrical System

question: In flight the ALTERNATOR warning illuminates and the ammeter shows a discharge. What is the immediate consequence for the pilot?

options.text: The engine will stop within a few minutes because ignition depends on the alternator
All electrical services are lost instantly
Electrical services now run from the battery only, for a limited time
Nothing changes, because the battery charges the system in flight

explanation: With the alternator offline the battery becomes the only source of electrical power, so endurance is limited and non-essential loads should be shed and a landing planned. The engine itself keeps running: ignition is provided by engine-driven magnetos, which are independent of the aircraft electrical system.
reference: Airplane Flight Manual, Section 3 - Emergency Procedures

question: What is the main system voltage and primary electrical power source described for the DA 40 D TDI?

options.text: A 28V DC system powered by a permanent-magnet magneto generator
A 14V DC system powered by a 60 or 70 amp alternator
A 12V AC system powered by a belt-driven dynamo
A 24V DC dual-alternator layout with split-phase charging

explanation: On this description the aircraft runs a 14V DC network, normally supplied by a single 60 or 70 amp engine-driven alternator that also recharges the batteries.

question: What distinct batteries does this description give the DA 40 D TDI, and what does each do?

options.text: One large lead-acid battery that powers everything
A Main Battery for starting and systems, an ECU backup battery pack for the FADEC, and a separate Emergency Battery for backup avionics
A lithium-ion propulsion battery and a Ni-Cad avionics backup block
Two identical batteries that cycle automatically every 15 minutes

explanation: On this description, the Main Battery feeds the starter and general buses, a dedicated ECU backup battery pack is reserved for the engine computers, and a separate Emergency Battery powers the backup attitude instrument.

question: In this description, what keeps the engine running if the alternator fails completely in flight?

options.text: The engine switches to a mechanical carburettor and magneto ignition
The FADEC shuts down two cylinders automatically to conserve electricity
The FADEC keeps drawing power from the Main Battery, then from its own dedicated ECU backup batteries if that depletes
A small wind turbine deploys from the wing to charge the system

explanation: Because this FADEC-controlled engine needs electrical power for its injectors and computer, a total alternator failure forces the system onto the Main Battery, with the ECU backup batteries stepping in if that battery is exhausted.

question: For how long are the ECU backup batteries described as able to power the FADEC after a total Main Battery/alternator failure?

options.text: Exactly 5 minutes
15 minutes, provided the radio is off
At least 30 minutes
2 hours in cold weather

explanation: On this description, the ECU backup batteries are sized to power both engine computer channels for at least 30 minutes, enough for an emergency descent and landing at a nearby field.

question: What is the purpose of an Essential Bus switch, and when would a pilot use it in this description?

options.text: It turns on cabin and strobe lighting for night operations
It manually sheds non-essential electrical loads to conserve the Main Battery during an alternator failure
It overrides the FADEC and forces the propeller governor to maximum RPM
It connects the fuel transfer pump directly to the starter motor

explanation: Selecting the Essential Bus during an alternator failure sheds heavy, non-critical loads so the remaining battery power is concentrated on the critical flight instruments and primary systems.

question: Why does this description give the DA 40 D TDI two separate master switches, Electric Master and Engine Master?

options.text: Electric Master is for the left wing and Engine Master for the right wing
Electric Master activates the main aircraft electrical system, while Engine Master enables the FADEC and fuel systems needed to run the engine
Engine Master is a purely mechanical backup for the fuel control valve
They are fully redundant; either one activates the whole aircraft

explanation: On this description, Electric Master connects the battery to the main buses, while Engine Master separately boots the FADEC computers, initialises the glow plugs for a cold start, and activates the electronic fuel systems.

question: What does it mean if both the FADEC 'ECU A' and 'ECU B' warning lights illuminate together in flight?

options.text: The landing gear failed to lock up
A severe, critical fault has occurred in the engine control system, or a total loss of primary electrical power is imminent
The fuel transfer pump has finished emptying the auxiliary tank
The aircraft has entered a thermal updraft

explanation: One ECU light alone means a minor fault switched control to the backup channel. Both lights together mean serious errors, or a critical power-supply failure, affect both channels at once, and engine failure may be imminent.

question: How does a pilot verify that the FADEC has no outstanding fault before takeoff, in this description?

options.text: By holding the FADEC test button for more than 30 seconds until the engine shuts off
By confirming no steady or flashing 'ECU A/B' caution flags remain after the pre-flight ECU run-up test
By formatting the SD card slot on the primary display
The FADEC's memory clears itself automatically whenever the fuel transfer pump cycles

explanation: On this description, a fault the FADEC detects is stored as a code with a caution light; the pre-flight ECU test exercises both computer channels, and a light that stays on or flashes afterward means a fault is latched and needs maintenance before flight.
